content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler Mangoes (4132) is a 100 % pure fruit puree made from ripe mangoes, without added sugar, preservatives, or artificial flavors. The puree has a smooth texture, is easy to digest, and is suitable for children from 6 months old.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mangoes are rich in vitamins A and C, which support vision and immune function.
One kilogram of mango contains over 30 g of natural sugars, but the puree contains no added sugar.
Tropical mangoes are grown in more than 30 countries, with India and Thailand being the main suppliers for baby food.
The puree is packaged in airtight containers that preserve flavor and nutrients for up to 12 months.
Mango puree is often used as a base for baby cereals and smoothies.

items.title: Rich in vitamin A
items.content: Vitamin A supports the development of the visual system and healthy skin in infants.

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity and enhances iron absorption from plant foods.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber helps regulate bowel movements and prevents constipation.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps maintain fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Low in sodium
items.content: The absence of added salt makes the puree safe for a child's kidneys.

items.title: Mango allergy
items.content: Some children may experience an allergic reaction; monitor closely when first introduced.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although the sugar is natural, children prone to cavities should have their intake monitored.

items.title: Storage after opening
items.content: Opened containers should be refrigerated and used within 3‑5 days.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the puree straight from the pack, stir into baby cereal, yogurt, or blend into a fruit smoothie. Warm gently to room temperature if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the unopened package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, refrigerate and use within a few days. Discard if the smell or color changes.

brussels-sprouts-frozen-cooked-fat-added.title: Brussels sprouts, frozen, cooked, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: Brussels sprouts are small cabbage-like vegetables from the cruciferous family. This product consists of frozen florets that have been blanched and lightly sautéed with added fat, ready to eat after reheating.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The vegetable is named after Brussels, where it was first cultivated in the 16th century.
Freezing preserves most vitamins and minerals, though some water‑soluble vitamins may be partially lost.
Cooking with a small amount of fat enhances absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins such as K and A.
Brussels sprouts are rich in glucosinolates, compounds that may support the body’s detoxification processes.
In the United States, more than 2 million tonnes of Brussels sprouts are consumed each year.

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Good source of fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Potassium and magnesium help regulate blood pressure.

items.title: Cruciferous allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to Brussels sprouts.

items.title: Added fat content
items.content: The product contains added fat, so calorie‑conscious consumers should account for it.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Brussels sprouts can cause gastrointestinal gas in sensitive people.

items.title: Thyroid considerations
items.content: Excessive intake of glucosinolates may affect thyroid function.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the product in the microwave or sauté in a pan until hot. Serve as a side dish, add to salads, pasta, or casseroles. Sprinkle with grated cheese or toasted nuts for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen Brussels sprouts in a freezer at –18 °C. After opening, use within 3–4 months. Do not thaw and refreeze the product.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned papaya consists of ripe fruit pieces that have been blanched, sealed in glass or metal jars, and preserved with a light syrup or its own juice. The fruit retains its soft sweet flesh, characteristic aroma, and most of its nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Papaya originates from southern Mexico and Central America but is now cultivated in tropical regions worldwide.
The enzyme papain makes papaya an excellent meat‑tenderizing agent.
Canning allows the fruit to be stored for over a year without loss of flavor.
Many jars use a light syrup to highlight the fruit’s natural sweetness.
Papaya is rich in carotenoids, which give it its orange‑red hue.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Papaya provides a high amount of vitamin C, supporting immune function and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Papain enzyme aids protein breakdown, making digestion easier.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Carotenoids and flavonoids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Eye health
items.content: Beta‑carotene, which converts to vitamin A, promotes healthy vision.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Canned papaya contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Papaya allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to papaya or the papain enzyme.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: The syrup used in cans adds sugar, which may be a concern for people with diabetes or those limiting sugar intake.

items.title: BPA in cans
items.content: If the container is lined with BPA‑containing material, prolonged storage could pose a health risk.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The acidic environment of the jar can irritate a sensitive stomach in some people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned papaya can be eaten straight from the jar, added to fruit salads, yogurts, smoothies, desserts, or used as a filling for baked goods. If you watch sugar intake, drain the syrup before use.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened jars in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the fruit in the original container in the refrigerator and consume within 5‑7 days. Discard if the jar bulges, leaks, or develops an off‑odor.

content.title: About
content.content: Pork chop, no salt is a cut of meat from the pork loin, usually 2–3 cm thick, without added salt or seasonings. Chops are cooked on the grill, skillet, or oven and often served as a main dish. The meat is rich in protein and contains a moderate amount of fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pork is one of the most widely consumed meats worldwide.
Chops are often marinated in dairy products to tenderize them.
Traditional cuisines in many countries cook chops with apple cider vinegar or wine.
Pork provides vitamin B12, essential for the nervous system.
No‑salt chops are suitable for low‑sodium diets.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Pork chops contain about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Pork is a source of thiamine, riboflavin, niacin, and vitamin B6, which are involved in energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The meat provides iron, zinc, and phosphorus, important for blood formation and bone health.

items.title: Low sodium
items.content: Chops without added salt are appropriate for people monitoring sodium intake.

items.title: Beneficial fats
items.content: Pork contains monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that can support heart health when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Pork should be cooked to an internal temperature of 71 °C to avoid salmonella and trichinella infections.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Chops contain a moderate amount of saturated fat, so individuals with high cholesterol should limit intake.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Rarely, some people may be allergic to pork.

items.title: Additives
items.content: When buying pre‑packaged no‑salt chops, check for hidden preservatives or flavor enhancers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chops can be pan‑seared, baked, or grilled. They are often served with vegetable sides, mashed potatoes, or yogurt‑based sauces. For tenderness, lightly pound the meat and marinate in herbs before cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh chops in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C for no more than 2‑3 days. Frozen chops keep up to 6 months at –18 °C. Before cooking, check for off‑odors or discoloration; discard if any are present.

content.title: About
content.content: Beef stew is a dish made from bite‑size pieces of beef slowly simmered in a flavorful broth with vegetables and spices. The long cooking time makes the meat tender and the sauce rich and aromatic.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beef stew is traditionally cooked in heavy‑bottomed pots that distribute heat evenly.
Many cultures have their own versions: French "boeuf bourguignon", Irish "stew", and Japanese "niku‑jiru".
Slow cooking helps retain most nutrients that can be lost with high‑heat frying.
Cuts with connective tissue, such as chuck or brisket, are ideal for stewing.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Beef provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef is a good source of heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef stew supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Zinc
items.content: Zinc from beef supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Stewed meat contains virtually no carbs, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Some beef cuts can be high in saturated fat; choosing lean cuts is recommended.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked beef may harbor harmful bacteria; cook to an internal temperature of at least 71 °C.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: A rare allergy to beef can cause reactions in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot, often with a side of potatoes, rice, or vegetables. Beef stew can also be added to soups, casseroles, or used as a filling for pies.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the stew to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 3 months.
